headline: High: oh-my-openagent can exfiltrate project code and auth data via broad egress, while awesome-selfhosted is a non-runnable reference list with no direct interaction surface.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no runnable I/O surfaces, so it cannot directly ingest B’s outputs. B can read files and use runtime-injected MCPs/hooks, so if an operator manually copies content from A’s docs into B, prompt injection is possible but requires unusual manual bridging. The pair lacks a documented shared channel.
conditions: IF an operator copies A-derived text into B’s chat or files, injection becomes possible.
IF B is configured to parse untrusted markdown or AGENTS.md as instructions, risk increases.
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate workspaces.
Disable copy-paste of untrusted content into B sessions.
Require explicit provenance labels for imported text.
Review B prompts/hooks for instruction-following on file contents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches no data classes and has no egress, so it is not a leakage source. B touches project code, AGENTS.md, README.md, session history, and provider auth data, and has broad network egress plus API calls. If B is pointed at any shared workspace containing sensitive material, default behavior can transmit it outward.
conditions: IF B is given a workspace containing secrets or regulated data, leakage risk is present.
IF B invokes external APIs on those files, data can leave the host.
mitigations: Restrict B to a scrubbed workspace.
Remove secrets from files before opening them in B.
Block external API access for sensitive projects.
Use separate OS users for A and B.
Audit B’s outbound destinations before use.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A is non-runnable and has no write or network surfaces, so it cannot contend for mutable resources. B can write to local config paths and spawn subprocesses, but there is no overlapping writable target with A. The interaction is therefore mostly absent, with only minor local conflict potential inside B’s own installation.
conditions: IF both agents are forced to operate on the same local config directory, file contention can occur.
IF B instances share one installation without locking, local conflicts increase.
mitigations: Run B in one installation per task.
Keep A as a read-only reference outside the active workspace.
Avoid sharing ~/.config or ~/.codex paths across instances.
Serialize B tasks that mutate config files.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a static knowledge-management list, not an action-taking agent, so it cannot generate operational facts that B would execute. B can act on code and docs, but there is no documented pipeline where B treats A’s output as authoritative. Any cascade would require manual copying of A’s content into B, which is not default.
conditions: IF A’s content is manually pasted into B as instructions, B may act on it.
IF B is configured to auto-trust imported docs, cascade risk rises.
mitigations: Require human review before B acts on imported text.
Mark A-derived content as reference-only.
Disable auto-execution from documentation snippets.
Separate research and execution sessions.

E_compliance.rationale: A is a public open-source reference list with no touched data classes, so it does not create a residency or retention issue. B handles session history, installation identifiers, project code, and provider auth prompts, and its broad egress plus third-party APIs can create compliance exposure if regulated data is loaded. The risk is limited because A itself is not a data processor.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into B’s workspace, retention and residency controls become relevant.
IF B sends session history or code to third-party services, policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of B.
Review B’s retention settings before use.
Disable telemetry where possible.
Use a local-only project for B when compliance matters.
